extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and judges (patent infringement/damages)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for assessing patent infringement, validity as affected by novelty/utility/severity of claim breadth, and measures of damages; includes tests for sameness in principle, combination vs separate claims, severability, and the temporal scope of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity (same in principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The question to be determined is, whether they are, under the patent law, the same in substance, or, as it is usually called, the same in principle; superior utility settles that question. Two things are not the same under the patent law, when one is practically, substantially better than the other, and this improvement is not gained by the use of known mechanical equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare in practical utility and substance rather than mere form; a substantially better result that is not produced by known equivalents indicates non-sameness. (Examples and cases cited: Hill v. Thompson; Davis v. Palmer.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial vs colorable/formal change
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is, whether the change be colorable and formal, or substantial and essential; that is, whether it be such as would of itself support a patent. The jury must find whether what is new is essential, or useless, and a colorable evasion; whether, by reason of the change, the thing has acquired a new and distinct character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A change producing a new effect or enabling an old result in a more economical/beneficial manner can be patentable. Examples: substitution of circular for reciprocating saw; welding by rollers without a mandrill, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims: infringement only when full combination used
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent stands upon its subject-matter, and accordingly the question of infringement depends upon the use of that which is covered by the patent. A patent may be for a new combination, whether the particular parts or things constituting that combination be new or old. But where the patent is for a combination, and not for several and distinct improvements, it is no infringement to use any of the parts or things which go to make up the combination, if the combination itself be not used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is to the combination as such, defendants may use individual elements without infringement so long as the claimed combination is not employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct improvements: individual use can infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent is for several distinct improvements or things, and does not stand upon the combination of such things, then the use of any one of them will be an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, all such claimed improvements had to be new for the patent to stand; statutory and later developments (see Acts cited) affect severability — see next metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of multiple claimed improvements / whole-patent risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly it was necessary that the whole of the improvements claimed as such should be new; and if the novelty of any one of them failed, the action could not be sustained — the patent might be void on account of partial failure of the whole consideration on which it was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine rests on the idea the consideration (novelty of all parts) was entire; subsequent statutes (Act of July 4, 1836 and later) recognize defenses and permit that a patent be deemed valid for so much as is truly the invention of the patentee if material and definitely distinguishable, unless the specification was knowingly made too broad to defraud the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability / statutory carve-out for materially distinct parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A more recent statute has provided that the patent shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention or discovery as shall be truly and bonâ fide the invention or discovery of the patentee, if it is a material and substantial part of the thing patented, and is definitely distinguishable from the other parts which the patentee had no right to claim, notwithstanding the specification may be too broad, if it was so made by mistake, accident or inadvertence, and without any wilful default or intent to defraud or mislead the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaves former doctrine applicable where the claim was made too broad wilfully or with intent to deceive; courts will separate valid, distinguishable, material parts when made innocently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement and false suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: If any thing claimed as essential turn out to be useless, the patent is voidable, provided it was known to the patentee, at the time of enrolling his specification, to be useless, because he misleads the public by representing it to be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a part was later discovered not to be useful, that alone does not invalidate the patent unless there was a false suggestion at the time of grant. A patent for an entire machine useful on the whole remains valid even if some parts are useless, so long as there is no false suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent cannot be for an abstract principle; embodiment required
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a patent for a principle; a principle must be embodied and applied so as to afford some result of practical utility in the arts and manufactures ... it is that embodiment and application which is in reality the subject-matter of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent covers the embodiment/application (the practice founded upon the principle) not the bare scientific truth or law; if another clothes the spirit of an invention in a different body, it is a jury question whether that is a substantial adaptation of the same principle and therefore an imitation in substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-only claims require reduction to practice / new substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The method and the mode of doing a thing are the same, and it is impossible to support a patent for a method only, without having carried it into effect, and produced some new substance. 'Principle reduced into practice' means a practice founded on principle — the thing done or made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely abstract methods are insufficient; the inventive concept must be embodied in a manufacture or practical application to be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of damages — actual damages and court discretion to treble
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute: whenever in any action for damages for using or selling the thing whereof the exclusive right is secured by any patent... it shall be in the power of the court to render judgment for any sum above the amount found by such verdict as the actual damages sustained by the plaintiff, not exceeding three times the amount of thereof, according to the circumstances of the case. By the terms 'actual damages sustained by the plaintiff' are meant such damages as he can actually prove, and has in fact sustained, as contradistinguished from mere imaginary or vindictive damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may treble proven actual damages up to three times; actual damages must be provable and not speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of 'actual damages' — profits and plaintiff losses
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of infringement by an actual use of the plaintiff's invention — as by making and using a patented machine — give the value of such use during the time of the illegal user, that is to say, the amount of profits actually received by the defendant. To this, there should also be added all the losses to which the plaintiff has been subjected by the piracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper ingredients for jury consideration include price of the machine, nature, extent of use, profits of defendant, and particular losses of plaintiff (valere quantum valcant). Courts may leave damages to jury discretion rather than prescribe a single fixed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal damages when no actual damage shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Where merely the making of a patented machine is proved, and no actual damages have been sustained, nominal damages only should be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant made but did not use the infringing machine and plaintiff cannot prove quantifiable loss, award nominal damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of counsel fees and witness expenses as damages
rubrics_metrics.description: It was formerly doubted whether the jury were at liberty to allow, as part of the actual damage, the counsel fees and expenses of witnesses beyond the taxable costs, incurred by the plaintiff in vindicating his right. But it is now the established rule and practice to allow them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-taxable litigation expenses may be recovered as part of actual damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of infringement and effect of prior use/renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent cannot be infringed by anything done when the patent did not exist; it is no infringement to make or use a machine subsequently patented, before the patent is obtained. But when a patent is granted, the right in the subject-matter relates back to the time of the invention, so that the party who has practised the invention between the time of the discovery and the issuing of the patent, must cease to do so. Any acts of infringement done after the issuing of the patent will be ground for the recovery of damages. Acts done in violation of a patent which is surrendered and renewed... will be an infringement of the new and renewed patent if he continues the use after the renewal; and it seems that no notice of the renewal is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use before grant is not infringement until patent issues, but once granted the patentee may enjoin continuation and recover for acts after issuance; surrender/renewal may revive liability without separate notice if original patent known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery for infringement during exceptional record-gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may recover damages for an infringement during the time which intervened between the destruction of the patent office by fire... and the restoration of the records under the act of March 3, 1837.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special statutory/contextual circumstances (e.g., loss of records) do not necessarily bar recovery for infringements that occurred during the record gap.
